content: The Department of Energy's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) is a prominent research institution conducting unclassified scientific research. It is situated on the grounds of the University of California, Berkeley, in the Berkeley Hills, above the central campus. The laboratory is managed and operated by the University of California. The laboratory was originally established on August 26, 1931, as the Radiation Laboratory of the University of California by physicist Ernest Orlando Lawrence. It was created as a center for physics research, particularly focused on Lawrence's invention, the cyclotron, a particle accelerator for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939. During the 1930s, Lawrence worked to develop increasingly larger cyclotrons, securing funding from private philanthropists by promising advancements in chemotherapy using radioisotopes produced by these machines. In the early years, the laboratory faced competition in making fundamental discoveries, which led to closer collaboration between the cyclotroneers and theoretical physicists at Berkeley, including Robert Oppenheimer. By 1940, the lab moved to its current location in the Berkeley Hills due to the increasing size and potential hazards of its machines, such as the 184-inch cyclotron. During World War II, Lawrence played a key role in the Manhattan Project, the U.S. effort to develop the atomic bomb. Using the 184-inch cyclotron as a mass spectrometer, Lawrence and his colleagues developed the principle of electromagnetic uranium enrichment. This method was implemented in the calutrons at the Y-12 facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, contributing fissile material for the Little Boy bomb dropped on Hiroshima, Japan. After the war, Lawrence sought to maintain strong ties with the government and military. The lab became part of the Atomic Energy Commission's (now Department of Energy) National Laboratory system. However, in the early 1950s, Lawrence emphasized that the lab's primary focus would be unclassified research, with classified weapons research conducted at Los Alamos National Laboratory and the newly established Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, which he co-founded with Edward Teller. Following Lawrence's death in 1959, the lab was renamed the Ernest O. Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory, though it was often referred to as the Rad Lab or LBL. Over time, the name evolved to Berkeley Lab, and its formal name became the Ernest O. Lawrence National Laboratory. Since the 1950s, the lab has remained a major international center for physics research and has diversified into numerous scientific fields, including astrophysics, nuclear fusion, earth sciences, genomics, health physics, computer science, materials science, and environmental science. The lab hosts several National User Facilities, such as the Advanced Light Source, the National Center for Electron Microscopy, the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center, the Energy Sciences Network, and the Molecular Foundry. It spans 8 square kilometers in the Berkeley Hills and employs approximately 4,000 University of California staff, including 800 students. Each year, it also hosts over 3,000 guest researchers. Federal oversight is provided by about two dozen Department of Energy employees stationed at the lab. The lab's 17 scientific divisions are organized into areas such as Computing Sciences, Physical Sciences, Life and Environmental Sciences, and General Sciences. Many research projects involve collaboration across multiple divisions, integrating computational and engineering expertise with biosciences, general sciences, and energy sciences. The lab director, appointed by the Regents of the University of California, reports to the university president. The current director is Steve Chu. Although governed independently of the Berkeley campus, the lab maintains close ties with the university. Over 200 LBNL researchers hold joint appointments as Berkeley faculty, and more than 500 Berkeley graduate students conduct research at the lab. LBNL is also a partner in the Joint Genome Institute, founded in 1997 to advance genome mapping, DNA sequencing, technology development, and information sciences. The lab manages the Department of Energy's high-speed research network, ESnet. Since World War II, the lab has achieved numerous scientific milestones, including the observation of the antiproton, the discovery of several transuranic elements, and the confirmation of the accelerating universe. Eleven researchers affiliated with the lab have received Nobel Prizes, including Ernest Lawrence, Glenn T. Seaborg, Edwin M. McMillan, Owen Chamberlain, Emilio G. Segrè, Donald A. Glaser, Melvin Calvin, Luis W. Alvarez, Yuan T. Lee, Steve Chu, and George F. Smoot. Elements discovered by lab physicists include astatine, neptunium, plutonium, curium, americium, berkelium, californium, einsteinium, fermium, mendelevium, nobelium, lawrencium, dubnium, and seaborgium. Some of these elements are named after the lab or its principal scientists. The lab has also contributed to technological advancements, such as the development of networking tools like libpcap, tcpdump, and traceroute by its Network Engineering Group. In 2002, the lab faced a major scandal when fabricated evidence by researcher Victor Ninov led to the retraction of two articles claiming the creation of elements ununoctium and ununhexium. This incident became one of the most significant controversies in physics at the time.
